facts.statehood_note: The first state to let women vote; Wyoming Territory had granted women the vote in 1869.
facts.nickname: The Equality State (official); also the Cowboy State
facts.name_origin: "Wyoming" was first the name of a valley in Pennsylvania. It comes from the Munsee Delaware language and means "at the big plains." Representative James Mitchell Ashley of Ohio suggested it for this region in 1865, and Congress chose it over the name "Lincoln" in 1868.

government.chambers: Wyoming Senate (31 senators, 4-year terms) and Wyoming House of Representatives (62 representatives, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term; limited to eight years in any sixteen-year period)
government.courts: Wyoming Supreme Court (5 justices). Each justice is appointed by the governor from three nominees chosen by a judicial nominating commission, serves an eight-year term, and then stands in retention elections. Wyoming has no intermediate court of appeals, so appeals go straight from the district courts to the Supreme Court.
government.constitution: Adopted by a convention at Cheyenne on September 30, 1889, and ratified by voters on November 5, 1889. It guaranteed women equal voting rights and included a pioneering article on water rights.
government.kid_line: "The rights of citizens of the State of Wyoming to vote and hold office shall not be denied or abridged on account of sex." (Wyoming Constitution, Article 6, Section 1)

long_ago.nation: Ancient hunters (Clovis, Folsom, and Plano cultures)
long_ago.about: People have lived in Wyoming for about 13,000 years; their stone spear points have been found throughout the state. Evidence in Yellowstone shows people were part of huge trade networks across the continent by about 1,000 years ago.
The Shoshone largely controlled much of western Wyoming. Shoshone place names across the Bighorn Basin show how well they knew lands east of the Wind River Basin.
By the mid-1800s the Crow were the leading nation in the Wind River Valley and Absaroka Range, using the area as winter range. Their name for the Green River means "sage hen river."
The Arapaho knew the Wind River Basin well and called the Wind River/Bighorn River Hotee Niicie, "mountain sheep river," for the many bighorn sheep there.
Plains nations recorded in the Wind River Basin after 1800, along with the Shoshone, Crow, Arapaho, and Blackfeet, drawn partly by food: trappers described herds of tens of thousands of bison there.

today.about: Federally recognized (listed as the Shoshone Tribe of the Wind River Reservation); shares the Wind River Indian Reservation, headquartered at Fort Washakie.

Federally recognized (listed as the Arapahoe Tribe of the Wind River Reservation); in the winter of 1878–79 the U.S. Army brought the Northern Arapaho to the Shoshone's Fort Washakie Agency, at first as a temporary placement.

first_peoples.today_note: Wyoming has two federally recognized tribes, the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho, who share the Wind River Indian Reservation (about 2.2 million acres in Fremont and Hot Springs Counties), the seventh-largest reservation in the United States by area.
sites: Devils Tower National Monument: ancient peoples lived around the Tower for thousands of years, and their descendants still hold ceremonies connected to it
Wind River Indian Reservation and Fort Washakie, named for the Shoshone leader Washakie
Yellowstone National Park: evidence of continent-wide Native trade networks about 1,000 years old

history.event: Ancient hunters of the Clovis, Folsom, and Plano cultures live in the region and leave stone spear points across Wyoming.
Native people in the Yellowstone area are part of huge trading networks reaching across the continent.

Nations including the Shoshone, Crow, Arapaho, Cheyenne, Lakota, Blackfeet, Bannock, and Ute live and hunt in the region, following great bison herds. French-Canadian trappers come to trade, leaving names like Téton and La Ramie.

John Colter, a former member of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, travels through Jackson Hole and the Yellowstone region, likely the first European American to see them. Few people believed his stories of hot springs and geysers.
Robert Stuart's party finds South Pass, which the Oregon Trail later follows. From 1840 to 1859, over 350,000 emigrants cross Wyoming on the Oregon, Mormon, and California Trails.
The United States and Plains nations, including a Shoshone band led by Washakie, meet for the first Treaty of Fort Laramie, meant to keep peace along the trails.

Settlers open the Bozeman Trail through the Powder River Country, on lands promised to Native nations. Fighting grows into Red Cloud's War, the first major war between the United States and Wyoming's nations. The 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie ends it by closing the Powder River Country to whites, and the 1868 Fort Bridger Treaty sets the Wind River Valley aside for the Shoshone.
The Union Pacific Railroad reaches Cheyenne in 1867, and Congress creates Wyoming Territory on July 25, 1868.

On December 10, 1869, Wyoming Territory becomes the first territory to give women the right to vote. In 1870 women serve on juries in Laramie, Esther Hobart Morris becomes the nation's first woman justice of the peace, and Louisa Swain votes in Laramie.
Yellowstone becomes the world's first national park.

Miners break the 1868 treaty by entering the Black Hills, leading to the Black Hills War (1876). In the winter of 1878–79, the U.S. Army moves the Northern Arapaho to the Shoshone's Fort Washakie Agency, next to their historic enemies.
In the Rock Springs massacre on September 2, European immigrant miners kill at least 28 Chinese immigrant miners and burn 78 of their homes; U.S. Army troops are sent in.
Wyoming writes its constitution (ratified November 5, 1889) and becomes the 44th state on July 10, 1890, the first state where women can vote.

trailblazers.name: Washakie
trailblazers.text: Washakie led a band of Shoshone to the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty council and was seen as head of the Eastern Shoshone until his death. He signed treaties at Fort Bridger in 1863 and 1868, securing the Wind River homeland where his people still live. Fort Washakie was renamed in his honor in 1878.

trailblazers.name: Black Coal (Wo'óoseinee')
trailblazers.text: Black Coal fought in the Powder River Country in the 1860s, then worked as a go-between with the United States. He traveled to Washington, D.C., in 1877 to seek a permanent home for his people, and spent the rest of his life working to secure the Northern Arapaho's right to live on the Wind River Reservation, where his band settled at the forks of the Wind and Popo Agie Rivers.

trailblazers.name: Louisa Swain
trailblazers.text: On September 6, 1870, in Laramie, Louisa Swain became the first woman in the United States to vote in a general election after New Jersey took away women's votes in 1807. Born in Norfolk, Virginia, she lived in the Charleston Orphan House in South Carolina after her mother died.

trailblazers.name: Esther Hobart Morris
trailblazers.text: On February 14, 1870, in South Pass City, Esther Hobart Morris began serving as the first woman justice of the peace in the United States. She was appointed after the previous justice quit in protest of Wyoming's new law letting women vote.

trailblazers.name: William Jefferson Hardin
trailblazers.text: William Jefferson Hardin grew up in Kentucky, took part in the California Gold Rush, and briefly served in a Union Army unit during the Civil War. In 1879 he became the first African American member of the Wyoming Legislature, serving in the territorial House until 1883.

trailblazers.name: Nellie Tayloe Ross
trailblazers.text: Elected in 1924, Nellie Tayloe Ross became the first woman governor in the United States, taking office in January 1925. In 1933 she became the first woman director of the U.S. Mint, serving until 1953.

landforms: Rocky Mountains, including the Wind River Range with Gannett Peak, the highest point (13,804 feet)
Absaroka, Owl Creek, and Gros Ventre Ranges
Laramie, Snowy, and Sierra Madre Ranges
Big Horn Basin and Wind River Basin
geography.regions: The Great Plains meet the Rocky Mountains in Wyoming: the western half is mountain ranges and basins, and the eastern half is high-elevation prairie called the High Plains. The Continental Divide runs north to south through the middle.

ecosystems.name: Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem
ecosystems.about: At 28,000 square miles, it is one of the largest nearly intact temperate-zone ecosystems on Earth. Yellowstone is home to 67 kinds of mammals, 285 birds, 16 fish, 5 amphibians, and 6 reptiles.

ecosystems.name: Hot springs and geysers
ecosystems.about: Trillions of tiny heat-loving microorganisms called thermophiles live in Yellowstone's hot springs, forming bright mats of color.

ecosystems.name: High Plains prairie
ecosystems.about: The eastern half of the state is high, dry prairie. After 1800, trappers described herds of tens of thousands of bison in the Wind River Basin; the American bison is now the state mammal.

ecosystems.name: Dry basins
ecosystems.about: Low areas like the Big Horn Basin get only 5–8 inches of rain a year, making them nearly true deserts.

science.weather: Dry and windy, with big temperature swings; much of the state gets less than 10 inches of rain a year, while some mountains get 200 inches or more of snow. Chinook winds can bring sudden warm spells in winter. The record high is 114°F at Basin (1900) and the record low is −66°F at Riverside (1933). Thunderstorms peak in late spring and early summer, and the southeastern corner has the most (usually small) tornadoes.
science.resources: Mining and tourism drive Wyoming's economy: it is the nation's top coal producer and produces oil, natural gas, and trona (about 25% of the world's supply). Ranching and farming produce livestock, hay, barley, sugar beets, wheat, and wool.
science.highlight: Yellowstone National Park, created in 1872 as the world's first national park, protects more than 10,000 hydrothermal features, including more than 500 geysers, about half of the world's active geysers.

g3_ss.title: Wyoming's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Map Cheyenne and the student's county among 23 counties; learn the Legislature, governor, and Supreme Court; read Article 6, Section 1 and talk about why Wyoming is the Equality State.

g3_ss.title: Wyoming's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho of the Wind River Reservation, and the Crow, Cheyenne, and Lakota who also hunted here; bison and how nations used them.

g3_ss.title: Wyoming Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Washakie, Louisa Swain, Esther Hobart Morris, William Jefferson Hardin, and Nellie Tayloe Ross; students design a "first" medal for each.

g45_ss.title: Wyoming's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: 13,000 years of people, Yellowstone trade networks, Shoshone, Crow, and Arapaho homelands, and the Wind River Reservation today.

g45_ss.title: Trails, Treaties, and Trappers
g45_ss.plan: Fur trappers, South Pass and the emigrant trails, the Fort Laramie and Fort Bridger treaties, Red Cloud's War, and how treaties were broken.

g45_ss.title: Rails to Statehood, 1867–1890
g45_ss.plan: The Union Pacific, women's suffrage in 1869, the Rock Springs massacre of Chinese miners, the Arapaho move to Wind River, and statehood in 1890.

g3_sci.title: Geysers and Hot Springs
g3_sci.plan: What makes a geyser erupt; colorful thermophiles; model a geyser with a bottle and water.

g3_sci.title: Life on the High Plains
g3_sci.plan: Bison, meadowlarks, cottonwoods, and wind; how plants and animals live with little rain.

g3_sci.title: Mountains and the Continental Divide
g3_sci.plan: Which way rivers flow on each side of the Divide; build a simple divide model with a folded paper and water drops.

g45_sci.title: Yellowstone's Volcano
g45_sci.plan: How a volcano, earthquakes, and glaciers shaped Yellowstone; hydrothermal features and how scientists study extremophiles.

g45_sci.title: Dinosaurs and Fossils of Wyoming
g45_sci.plan: Triceratops (state dinosaur) and Knightia (state fossil); how fossils form and what they tell us about ancient environments.

g45_sci.title: Energy from the Ground
g45_sci.plan: Coal, oil, natural gas, and trona: how each forms, how it is mined, and its effects on land, water, and air.
